newsitem.title: USA: IMF sees positive outlook for developing countries.
newsitem.headline: IMF sees positive outlook for developing countries.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund on Wednesday gave optimistic economic forecasts for developing and "transition" countries in 1997 and 1998 although it also noted some clouds on the horizon.

The World Economic Outlook report, released ahead of next week's IMF/World Bank joint spring meeting, raised slightly most of the growth projections it had made in October for those groups of countries.
"In many of the dynamic emerging market countries, there was a desirable moderation in growth and inflation in 1996, which should allow their expansions to be sustained in the period ahead," it said.
The report said growth had picked up in the Latin American countries worst hit by Mexico's financial crisis in 1995.

Economic activity also picked up in the Middle East and Africa, while the so-called "transition" countries, taken as a group, were expected to post positive growth in 1997 for the first time since the collapse of central planning.

The report's tables of projections for economic growth showed that the IMF expected developing countries, as a group, to post rates of 6.6 percent in 1997 and 6.5 percent in 1998, against a 6.5 percent increase last year.
Inflation in that group should also continue to ease from 13.1 percent in 1996 to 9.7 percent this year and 8.5 percent in 1998, the report said.
Broken down by regions, Asia was slated to remain the top performer in economic growth, posting an 8.3 percent increase in 1997 and and a 7.7 percent rise next year, against last year's 8.2 percent.

The Western Hemisphere, which for the IMF encompasses Latin America and the Caribbean, should post economic growth rates of 4.4 percent this year and 5.1 percent next year, up from 3.5 percent in 1996.
Developing countries in Africa were expected to grow by about 4.7 percent this year and 4.8 percent in 1998, slightly below last year's 5.0 percent.
Emerging economies in the Middle East could increase by 3.9 percent this year and the next, against last year's 4.5 percent.
For the "transition" countries the IMF forecast growth rates of 3.0 percent in 1997 and 4.8 percent in 1998, up from last year's 0.1 percent and a 0.8 percent decrease in 1995.
Inflation in that group should also continue to abate from nearly 120 percent in 1995 and 40.4 percent last year to 30.7 percent this year and 11.6 percent in 1998.
"... Despite these grounds for optimism, it is important to recognize that contrasts in economic performance across countries have become starker in recent years," the IMF said.

While an increasing number of developing nations are benefitting from sound fiscal policies and market-oriented economic reforms, some countries have suffered setbacks and others remain vulnerable to swings in investor sentiment.
Some of the poorest have lagged badly and risk being left out of the mainstream of economic progress, it said.

"Among the transition countries, the contrasts have also widened between some of the early, relatively successful reformers and countries that have started adjustment and reform later and with less determination and consistency," it added.

Some of the factors that could mar the outlook for developing and "transition" countries were beyond their control, such as the outcome of European plans for monetary union or a re-emergence of inflationary pressures in mature economies that could to lead to sharp interest rate rises.

Closer to home for the smaller economies, the IMF warned that the reliance on capital inflows by some countries and the recent narrowing of interest spreads for loans to developing nations may not be sustainable.
It said the surge in capital flows to emerging markets in recent years reflected both the globalization of financial markets and the economic success of many recipient countries.

However, the IMF added that "caution is warranted since the global availability of these flows and their cost are vulnerable to higher global interest rates and to adverse developments affecting systemically important capital-importing countries".
The IMF also repeated its concern over the fragility of banking system in a broad spectrum of countries stemming from excessive credit expansion and inadequate supervision.

"In some emerging market countries, banking sector difficulties linked to significant exposure to foreign exchange risk have become more apparent following the reversal of capital flows from abroad," it said.
Mexico and Argentina suffered major banking crises in 1995 in the wake of the peso debacle, which has been largely attributed to those countries' dependence on capital inflows at the time.
-- Peter Bate, Washington newsroom ((202) 898-8306))
